\chapter{Taking Leave}
\label{ch:ml-taking-leave}
\hlchaptermodality{50}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say when I am going and take my leave in Malayalam, using either of the two phrases the language builds for it.}

Complete ML-C50-farewell and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ippōḷ]{\ml{ഇപ്പോൾ} (ippōḷ) — now}

\label{lesson:ML-C50-now}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{orupakṣē} mean, and what did \emph{aṅṅane} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഇപ്പോൾ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഇപ്പോൾ}} (\emph{ippōḷ}) — \textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}.

The pointing pattern again, and this time on time rather than manner. \emph{i-} is the near one, so \ml{ഇപ്പോൾ} is 'at this time'. Its far partner \ml{അപ്പോൾ} (\emph{appōḷ}) is 'at that time, then', and the two differ by one letter.

Tamil says \ta{இப்போது} (\emph{ippōtu}) — the same two pieces, put together the same way.

The word ends on \ml{ൾ}, the chillu already met at the end of \ml{നിങ്ങൾ}. Kannada's word for now, \ka{ಈಗ} (\emph{īga}), is built from its own near-pointer and shares nothing else with this one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for going away.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ippōḷ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ippōḷ}, then \emph{aṅṅane}, and hear the near and the far openers side by side
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ഇപ്പോൾ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maṟṟannāḷ]{\ml{മറ്റന്നാൾ} (maṟṟannāḷ) — the day after tomorrow}

\label{lesson:ML-C50-day-after}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ippōḷ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മറ്റന്നാൾ}}
\textbf{\ml{മറ്റന്നാൾ}} (\emph{maṟṟannāḷ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.

Three pieces, and the last of them this book has already taught: \ml{നാൾ}, the native day-word. Before it sits \ml{മറ്റ്} (\emph{maṟṟŭ}), 'other', and a middle piece pointing at a particular day. Put together: the other day along.

Malayalam does not stop there. There is a word for the day after that one as well, and speakers use it without ceremony, where an English speaker would give up and name a date.

Kannada builds its own with the same idea and different parts, \ka{ನಾಡಿದ್ದು} (\emph{nāḍiddu}), and its day-word is the cousin of ours.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: now, and the day after tomorrow.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maṟṟannāḷ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ippōḷ}, then \emph{maṟṟannāḷ}, the nearest time and a far one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മറ്റന്നാൾ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yātra]{\ml{യാത്ര} (yātra) — a journey}

\label{lesson:ML-C50-journey}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maṟṟannāḷ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{യാത്ര}}
\textbf{\ml{യാത്ര}} (\emph{yātra}) — \textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{yātrā}, off a root meaning simply 'to go'. A journey is a going, with a noun ending on it.

Malayalam then does something with the word that Sanskrit did not: \ml{യാത്ര} \ml{പറയുക}, literally 'to say journey', is how a speaker takes leave of a household. The noun for travelling became the verb phrase for saying goodbye, because what you announce at the door is that you are going.

Kannada's \ka{ಪ್ರಯಾಣ} (\emph{prayāṇa}) is the same root with a prefix in front of it — a going-forth. The sisters borrowed from the same shelf and reached for neighbouring jars.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. Now, the day after tomorrow, a journey.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{yātra}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{yātra}, then \emph{yātra paṟayuka}, the noun and the leave-taking built on it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{യാത്ര} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puṟappeṭuka]{\ml{പുറപ്പെടുക} (puṟappeṭuka) — to set out}

\label{lesson:ML-C50-set-out}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{yātra} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പുറപ്പെടുക}}
\textbf{\ml{പുറപ്പെടുക}} (\emph{puṟappeṭuka}) — \textquotedblleft{}to set out\textquotedblright{}.

A compound with its seam showing. \ml{പുറം} (\emph{puṟaṁ}) is 'the outside, the back'; Tamil has \ta{புறம்} with the same sense. The second piece is the ordinary verb of falling or happening. Together, roughly, 'to come to be outside' — which is what setting out is.

Malayalam builds a great many verbs this way, a noun and a light verb sitting next to each other, and this book has already shown one: the work-verb made of 'work' plus 'do'.

Kannada says \ka{ಹೊರಡು} (\emph{horaḍu}), built on its own outside-word, and that word begins with the \emph{h} where ours begins with a \emph{p}. The shift turns up again.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. Now, the day after tomorrow, a journey, setting out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puṟappeṭuka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{puṟappeṭuka}, then \emph{jōli ceyyuka}, two verbs built the same way
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പുറപ്പെടുക} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}to set out\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viṭa]{\ml{വിട} (viṭa) — leave, a farewell}

\label{lesson:ML-C50-farewell}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{puṟappeṭuka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വിട}}
\textbf{\ml{വിട}} (\emph{viṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}leave, a farewell\textquotedblright{}.

A short word off a plain verb: \ml{വിടുക} (\emph{viṭuka}) is 'to let go, to release'. \ml{വിട} is the letting-go itself.

And it is used exactly as the journey-word was: \ml{വിട} \ml{പറയുക}, 'to say farewell'. Malayalam has two ways to announce a departure, one naming the going and one naming the release, and both are built by hanging the speaking-verb off a noun.

Kannada's word here, \ka{ಬೀಳ್ಕೊಡುಗೆ} (\emph{bīḷkoḍuge}), is longer and made of its own native parts — a giving of leave. Three languages could hardly agree less on how to say goodbye, and each of them is transparent once opened.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: now, the day after tomorrow, a journey, setting out, a farewell.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{ippōḷ}, \emph{maṟṟannāḷ}, \emph{yātra}, \emph{puṟappeṭuka}, \emph{viṭa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വിട} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}leave, a farewell\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
